Where it began

Ajinkya Rahane was born in 1988 in Ashwi Khurd, a village in Maharashtra, and grew up in Dombivli, near Mumbai. When he was seven his father took him to a small coaching camp that played on a matting pitch, and from seventeen he was coached by the former India batter Pravin Amre.

He made a hundred on his first-class debut for Mumbai, aged nineteen, and the runs kept coming. In one Ranji Trophy season he passed a thousand, helping Mumbai to yet another title.

The player

His Test debut came against Australia in Delhi in March 2013, after a long spell of waiting in the squad. His first Test hundred followed in Wellington early in 2014, and later that year he made another at Lord's on his first appearance there, a hundred that rescued India on a green pitch.

He played 85 Tests from 2013 to 2023, making 5,077 runs at 38.46 with 12 hundreds and 26 fifties, and a best of 188 against New Zealand at Indore. In Delhi in 2015 he scored a hundred in each innings of the same Test. He also held 102 catches, eight of them in a single Test in Sri Lanka, a world record at the time.

What made him special

Rahane was at his best when the going was hardest. His runs in South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia earned him a name as a batter for difficult places, and his calm manner hid a steely mind.

His finest hour came as captain in Australia in 2020–21. Leading a side missing many first-choice players, he made a hundred in the second Test to bring India level, and India went on to win at Brisbane and take the series 2–1. In six Tests in charge India won four and lost none.

If there was a gap in his game, it was that his touch could come and go. When it came, though, it usually arrived in the matches that mattered most.

Away from the middle

He received the Arjuna Award in 2016. In the IPL he opened with Rahul Dravid at Rajasthan, who helped turn a shy Test specialist into a batter for every format, and in 2023 he won his first IPL title with Chennai. He later captained Kolkata, and he retired from all professional cricket in July 2026.

And finally

Rahane bats and bowls right-handed but writes with his left hand. It seems fitting for a cricketer who was always happy to do things a little differently, and quietly.
